But they sit cool in the cool shade, where the sun does not burn on the steps. They want everything to be merely spectators, just like those who stand in the street and gape at passersby. Thus do they also wait and gape at the thoughts which others have thought.

This is a radical idea but very true: you go to university not to learn how to think but to fall into ignorance. Why? Because professors there—priests there—have departed from reality, choosing a life of comfort, ease, and pleasure. As a result, they can't know anything. True knowledge can only be found in the everyday, with ordinary people.

That's where God is. The universe are constructed to be away from God; they are temples for the comfort of priests. So if you want true knowledge, go out into the world and talk to other people. Suffer.

That’s it. You can understand the beauty and power of Zoroastrianism. I really do believe this: Nishi was channeling Zoroaster, but in a way for the common mind. The thing about Asha is that it's always changing. The Asha that was true 3,000 years ago is not the same as the Asha that’s true today. What’s important to understand is that Asha is constantly coming.

So you have to constantly work towards it; there’s no endpoint to Asha. Asha will be different for everyone, but if everyone's moving towards Asha, then the world becomes a more virtuous, better place, and a more just place.

Um, any questions guys? Last class I gave a lecture on the Bible and made a mistake in my discussion about the story of the patriarchs. Specifically, between the love story of Rachel and Jacob, I said that Jacob had to work seven years for Rachel after his marriage to Leah. But as Cole tells me, actually, the Bible says that Laban, the father, gave Rachel to Jacob right away, but then Jacob had to work seven years to pay off a debt. Thank you to Cole for correcting the error.

In fact, I probably made many small errors in my lecture and make mistakes every class. So, I apologize for that. But this class is about questions, not answers. What makes this class interesting and special is that we're always asking hard questions: what does it mean to be human? Where do we come from? Why are we here? Where are we going?

We’re always asking these questions because they matter. Second thing is that I'm constantly in the process of becoming, trying to discover answers. For example, before I didn’t know about Zoroastrianism and made mistakes. So for instance, I said Christianity was the first monistic religion last semester; now I recognize it's actually Zorashinism.

I'm constantly discovering and growing, so we continue to speculate and explore together. If you don't like what I say in this class or my opinion, just wait a year or two; I'll probably change my opinion. Because that’s what true knowledge is about: if you want to pursue knowledge, be willing to destroy yourself to burn yourself into ashes so that you can build yourself anew.

This class is not about giving easy answers or facts to memorize; it's about asking questions that help you understand yourself and the world around you. This class is about conversation, dialogue, and debate.
